title: A Republican Lawmaker Wants to Codify the $100,000 H-1B Fee That a Judge Just Killed. Congress May Succeed Where Trump Failed.
excerpt: Utah Rep. Mike Kennedy's PROTECT Act would require H-1B applicants to pay $100,000 or the prevailing wage — whichever is higher — through legislation that no court can easily overturn.
body:
A Republican congressman is moving to resurrect Trump's $100,000 H-1B visa fee through legislation, just two days after a federal judge struck it down — a whiplash development that could reshape the cost of hiring Indian tech workers in the United States for years to come.

Utah Representative Mike Kennedy introduced the PROTECT Act on Tuesday, which would codify at the congressional level the same fee that U.S. District Judge Leo Sorokin vacated on Monday. Sorokin, an Obama appointee, ruled that the payment was a tax requiring congressional authorisation — a power that Article I of the Constitution reserves for lawmakers, not the president.

Kennedy's bill goes further than simply restoring the fee. It would require any H-1B applicant to pay either the prevailing wage rate or $100,000, whichever is greater, the congressman told the Daily Caller News Foundation. The legislation is explicitly designed to compel companies to prioritise hiring American workers before turning to foreign nationals.

**The stakes for Indian professionals are enormous.** Indians receive more than 70 per cent of all approved H-1B petitions annually — a dominance that has held since at least 2015. Before Trump's September 2025 proclamation hiked the fee, applications cost between $2,000 and $5,000 depending on the employer's size. The jump to $100,000 was designed to be a deterrent, and it worked: application volumes dropped sharply across the tech sector.

Judge Sorokin's ruling on Monday was hailed as a major win for the Indian tech community. New York Attorney General Letitia James, who led the lawsuit, said the court had "put an end to this administration's illegal attempt to destroy this critical program." The White House signalled it would appeal, pointing to a separate ruling by a Washington judge who upheld a nearly identical order.

But Kennedy's legislative push introduces a parallel threat. If the PROTECT Act passes Congress, it would be immune to the constitutional objection that sank Trump's executive action — because Congress, unlike the president, has the explicit power to levy fees and taxes.

**The politics are complicated.** Big Tech, which has historically been the programme's biggest champion, is also its biggest user. Amazon, Meta, and Microsoft led the list of approved new H-1B petitions in fiscal year 2025. But the AI boom has added a new wrinkle: Anthropic, OpenAI, and Nvidia have all ramped up H-1B applications, underscoring the fierce competition for AI talent that cannot easily be found domestically.

Trump himself has sent mixed signals. He called H-1B visas a "great programme" recently, telling reporters that the United States needs more migrant workers because American labourers are less skilled when it comes to producing microchips. That comment sat awkwardly alongside his administration's efforts to price foreign workers out of the market.

The timing adds another layer of complexity. Prime Minister Modi is expected to raise H-1B visa issues directly with Trump on the sidelines of the G7 summit in Evian-les-Bains next week, an Indian government source told Reuters. Trade, visas, and energy cooperation are all on the agenda for what would be the first face-to-face meeting between the two leaders since last year's India-Pakistan conflict.

For the roughly 600,000 Indian nationals currently in the H-1B pipeline — and the thousands of Indian IT firms that depend on the programme — the next few months will determine whether a federal judge's ruling holds, or whether Congress builds a wall that no court can knock down.

*Sources: Daily Caller News Foundation, Reuters, CNN, USA Today, The Indian Eye*
